speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head U of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How much clean energy and carbon credits will we need to depend on in order to meet this target?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Government had indicated in its target submission to the United Nations (UN) that it will implement regulations, pricing and market policies to incentivise and enable all sectors of our economy to decarbonise.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Would the Minister please elaborate on these plans?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What has been the response from the business community so far?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What is the expected impact on our economy and competitiveness, considering that Singapore is only one of the 13 countries which had submitted climate change targets to UN?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, 97% of our primary emissions come from our power, industrial and transport sectors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What are the expected cost increases to businesses and consumers associated with carbon emissions reduction and which industries and types of businesses are expected to bear the bulk of the cost burden?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To achieve our longer-term 2035 and 2050 targets, will we be making any pivots from our current decarbonisation strategy?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And lastly, would the Minister provide updates on the import of clean energy, the progress of solar panel installations and the studies on the viability of hygrogen and small modular nuclear reactors?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But I would like to ask the National Climate Change Secretariat (NCCS) coordinating the whole-of-Government response about interaction between our circular economy outcomes, plans and targets with our national climate change targets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, I understand that products not made in Singapore, like agricultural imports, electronic imports, car imports and so on, are not counted under our carbon budget and, as such, are not covered under our nationally determined contribution (NDC).

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Does the Government have any mechanism to track this outsourced carbon?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Is reducing these emissions covered under any Government strategy, like the Zero-waste Masterplan?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: From reading our NDC, it seems that the Government is working to calculate some degree of carbon abatement via recycling, but does this reflect that we track our outsourced carbon?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The built environment sector analyses and aims to reduce such carbon in the embodied carbon calculations, which are key to determining the greenness of a green building.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Are other carbon intensive sectors, like marine and manufacturing, subject to such scrutiny?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The European Union (EU) carbon border adjustment mechanism broadly targets goods and precursors that seem to be carbon-intensive and prone to carbon leakage.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I am not advocating for such a tariff, are we doing the analysis?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In view of this, I hope that we can fundamentally change our whole-of-Government key performance indicators (KPIs) to shift the focus from gross domestic product (GDP) growth to development KPIs, which include the compatibility of our country, where 1.5°C warming, in accordance with the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If we are to use the term "green growth", it must be warranted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Not only do we as a country need to reduce the resource footprint per unit of GDP, we need to continuously reduce our resource footprint altogether and this includes not simply exporting pollution to other countries we trade with.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The demand for AI, especially generative AI, has been increasing exponentially in the past two years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With this comes a staggering increase in the energy intensity and by extension, carbon emissions intensity of AI-related activities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government should look into regulating the carbon footprint of the use and development of AI.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, not all AI models are the same.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The issue arises when companies of different sizes rush to integrate general purpose AI into their products and services, leading to such general-purpose AI models being deployed in an indiscriminate manner millions, if not billions, of times a day for tasks that users do not require the use of general-purpose AI, thereby causing emissions to add up quickly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As Singapore is positioning itself to become an AI hub, as well as a data centre hub, has this been taken into consideration in the 2035 NDC commitments?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government should start to look into developing voluntary guidelines and eventually mandating the reporting of energy consumptions by AI models.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This has already been recommended by the United Nations Environmental Programme and governments, including those in United States (US) and the EU, are actively discussing similar regulations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This would encourage developers to explore and adopt energy-efficient practices to reduce the carbon intensity of their products.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: AI developers will be pushed to use smaller task-specific AI models instead of large general-purpose models.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such regulation would also have ripple effects within the AI ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Like the sustainability reporting landscape, there will be increased demand for products and services that help support such disclosures.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Data centres in Singapore may start looking at developing hardware that can more easily show AI developers their energy consumption.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Downstream businesses would also be more discerning about the AI models they adopt, taking into account their energy consumption and emissions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By being an early adopter of such regulations, Singapore can enable local AI developers and related businesses to integrate carbon conscious practices early and stay ahead as global demand for sustainable AI solutions grows.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The UNFCCC secretariat is the UN entity tasked with supporting the global responses to the threat of climate change.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have been an active player in the international climate change negotiations and signed and ratified the Paris Agreement in 2016.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is part of our 2035 NDC submitted to the UNFCCC.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In its statement accompanying the submission, it is said that Singapore is a small low-lying island state, climate change is an existential challenge to us.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For our 2035 NDC, and I quote from the statement, "reflects both our commitment to climate action, as well as the significant uncertainties we face in our decarbonisation journey." The lower bound of 45 MtCO2e keeps us on a linear path towards our net-zero target in 2050.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has also committed itself to continue to work on "the range of mitigation measures available to us and explore other mitigation options to drive emissions reductions." These solutions have the potential to grow the green economy, create new jobs and generate new opportunities in the low-carbon world.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In 2022, we announced our climate targets to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 and reduction of emissions to around 60 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2030 after peaking emissions earlier.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are we on track to meet our 2030 target?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will we be making any pivots from our current decarbonisation strategy to achieve our longer-term target in 2035 and 2050?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How will the recent global developments, such as the US pulling out of the Paris Agreement, affect Singapore's climate goals?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Chairman, let me begin by declaring that I am a senior executive with a local enterprise and I deal with matters related to sustainability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Despite impeding global climate action due to geopolitical uncertainties, I am encouraged that Singapore remains committed towards climate action, taking critical and bold steps to shift our nation towards a low-carbon society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Climate change is evidently impacting our lives today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As a nation, we must be steadfast in our actions to fight against this existential threat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This target puts us on the right trajectory for Singapore to achieve net-zero by 2050.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, achieving this level of carbon abatement is no mean feat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Achieving such a level of abatement would require significant structural shifts in our infrastructure, economy and technological landscape.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We are already witnessing such a transition due to the Government's push to increase adoption of solar power and electric vehicles in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While these activities do contribute towards our decarbonisation efforts, similar deployment efforts would need to be needle-moving in other sectors as well to achieve the level of abatement mentioned earlier.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I acknowledge the Government's push to significantly increase electricity imports to Singapore by 2035.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, beyond electricity imports, does the Government aim to implement any significant initiatives or mandate the industrial sector to further support our decarbonisation targets?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: How can our local industries contribute towards such efforts to enable structural shifts beyond just relying on the reduction of Singapore's grid emission factor?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Further, how can the Government support them in such activities?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For Singapore to become a low-carbon economy and with limited access to low-cost renewable energy, we need to heavily rely on low-carbon energy technologies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Yet, many of which are still nascent or not at full commercial scale.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I commend the Government for continuously monitoring, developing and testing new low-carbon technologies, including in bolder areas, such as nuclear energy, to ensure Singapore pursues optimal pathways to achieve net-zero.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As we explore all these new technology frontiers, there are benefits to take stock of earlier studies and to reflect as a nation how we can collectively leverage upon these learnings.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Among the multiple studies on low-carbon energy technologies the Government has undertaken, can Minister share some of the key opportunities and challenges identified?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Within this portfolio of technologies studied, are there any promising ones which can be further scaled with partners and piloted before end of the decade?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Beyond technology considerations, many low-carbon solutions, including electricity imports, carbon capture and carbon markets, would require international cooperation before deployment can take place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I note that Singapore has been pursing discussions with multiple countries over the past few years, regarding these cooperation activities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Despite the global headwinds and geopolitics, I am heartened that Singapore remains fully committed to climate action, guided by science and facts.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The steps we are taking today would be the cornerstone for our future low-carbon economy, where Government, industry and citizens can work collaboratively to achieve a greener Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I speak as Chairman of the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Climate Change (IMCCC), which coordinates our policy and measures across all sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And with your permission, Sir, I will take clarifications immediately after this speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Paris Agreement in 2015 marked a breakthrough in global climate action, with countries pledging to keep global warming within 1.5°C.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Although there has been unevenness in implementation, we were generally pulling in the same direction as a global community.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: However, the US has recently pulled out of the Paris Agreement, for the second time.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This has prompted other countries, like Argentina and Indonesia, for example, to question the wisdom of maintaining their climate commitments.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak has asked how these global developments will affect Singapore's climate goals.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is quite natural for countries to ask why they should continue to make these difficult changes when others are not and whether their efforts will even result in any meaningful change, without the participation of bigger players.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singapore's Climate Ambassador, Mr Ravi Menon, gave a speech a week ago at Temasek's Ecosperity Conversations.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It provides a succinct and clear assessment of the global state of play on climate change, and I recommend that Members read it.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ambassador Menon points out that the main drivers of climate action are politics, economics and nature.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Green technology has advanced dramatically in the last two decades.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Several of these technologies are now mature and mainstream, and make economic sense.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They are not just cleaner but lower cost.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The average levelised cost of solar energy globally, for instance, is now 50% lower than that of fossil fuels.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This explains why two-thirds of global energy investment in 2024 went to clean energy technologies and infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Countries and businesses realise this, which is why despite political perturbations, there is now much greater momentum for decarbonisation than just a decade ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Most of the world's advanced economies have been investing in decarbonisation and steadily reducing emissions.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They recognise that the green transition is an increasingly important driver of growth and therefore crucial not just to the health of the globe, but also to the prosperity of their people.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Climate change is no longer a future threat.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Every country, all of us, can see this – drought, fires, floods, loss of crop yields, more severe storms.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The last 10 years have been the hottest years ever on record.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In short, the timeline to respond and adapt is being set, not by us, mere humans, but by nature.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Countries and businesses which lag behind will be forced to act eventually.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The longer they wait, the sharper and more disruptive a transition they will have to make.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is why Singapore remains fully committed to effective climate action.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We want to put ourselves in the best possible position for the long-term challenge and the opportunities that arise.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is heartening that Members from both sides of this House have expressed support for our ambitious climate action plan and in particular, this downward trajectory of emissions, which is going to be a major challenge.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our 2035 NDC also signals our resolve to help our economy stay competitive in a low-carbon world.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Having an ambitious target generates demand for new green investments and gives Singapore-based companies an edge in developing new low-carbon solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It also allows us to remain attractive to companies that are looking to decarbonise their operations, which are aligned with our own national goals.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At the same time, as an alternative-energy disadvantaged nation, having a target range reflects the practical reality that our pace of decarbonisation depends heavily on technological developments and international collaboration.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This range also recognises that we need some flexibility to manage the impact on our households and businesses while aligning with the pace of transition in the rest of the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Miss Chan, Dr Lim and Ms Poh asked about progress toward our 2030 NDC and new measures for our 2035 target.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This summarises where we are now and our journey to get to net zero by 2050.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are on track to meet our 2030 NDC.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This puts us on track to meet our target of at least two gigawatts-peak of solar deployment by 2030.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: To put this in context, our electrical power consumption today is around eight gigawatts.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Of course, eight gigawatts is not the same as gigawatts-peak, but this puts it into context.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are working towards all vehicles running on clean energy by 2040.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As of this year, we have ceased registrations of new diesel cars and taxis.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Electric vehicle (EV) charging points have been installed in about half of all Housing and Development Board (HDB) carparks.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Members would have seen them sprouting up all over your HDB carparks.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A third of all new car registrations are electric cars.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are also on track to electrify half of our public bus fleet by 2030.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We will redouble our efforts on such measures.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry, the Ministry of Transport, and the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment will say more about this during their respective Committees of Supply (COS).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Beyond these measures, we will need to step up efforts to study and advance a fuller suite of potential decarbonisation solutions – something which several Members asked about.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: One key enabler is our carbon tax, which was raised to $25 a tonne last year.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The carbon tax shapes behaviour across our economy, from consumers to businesses.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The carbon tax, in a way, is a proxy for the cost of emissions by users.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It reflects the cost to the economy and to the users for emitting carbon.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This applies across the board, whether it is industry, or whether it is AI data centres.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This then puts some inhibition on whether or not they will continue to have high emission levels and it applies a cost to the eventual users of all these services.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: At the same time, we do not just collect the carbon tax, we plough these tax revenues back into supporting businesses and households so that they can become greener.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: One example is the Building and Construction Authority's (BCA's) existing buildings incentive scheme for owners to retrofit their buildings to Green Mark energy efficiency standards.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It does not come from the collection of carbon tax, but we are doing Climate Vouchers as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Leader of the Opposition made some comments about that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Of course, we will have to watch what happens on the global scene.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am heartened that both sides of this House have expressed support for a broad-based carbon tax, with the Workers' Party advocating even higher carbon taxes even sooner.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We take such feedback seriously and look forward to their continued support when we adjust our carbon taxes in the future.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We will continue to assess where the optimal range is.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Our current tax rate is carefully calibrated to give our businesses and households time to adjust and to account for the maturation of green technologies that will allow us to decarbonise more efficiently.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We will also need to tap on cross-border solutions to overcome the limitations of being a dense and alternative-energy disadvantaged city-state.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is why we have been laying the crucial groundwork for the development of an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) regional power grid, which will facilitate cross-border electricity trading and increase regional energy resilience for all the countries in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Unlike electricity imports, credits are not limited by proximity, by distance and by physical connections.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: At the 2024 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP29) last year, we co-facilitated negotiations that delivered the full operationalisation of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And Minister Grace Fu played a major role in that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have also signed Implementation Agreements on Article 6 carbon credits with Papua New Guinea and Ghana and memoranda of understanding (MOUs) with more than 15 other countries.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Just this morning, we signed a new Implementation Agreement with Bhutan.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These win-win agreements will promote the development of carbon mitigation projects in these countries while helping us meet our emissions targets.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) represents another pathway for us – one that is necessary to reduce emissions from hard-to-abate sectors.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are currently working with industry players to study the viability of cross-border carbon capture and storage projects.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Achieving our longer-term targets will also require new and innovative solutions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And several of these new technologies are showing promise.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have begun to deploy biofuels, such as sustainable aviation fuel, which can be produced from food and agricultural waste.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are also studying the potential for wider adoption of biofuels in sectors such as electricity generation and transport.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are also building capabilities to deploy hydrogen and ammonia, including through small, pilot-scale projects, as we wait for these fuels to become commercially viable at scale.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In the longer term, as the Prime Minister stated in the Budget Speech, we are studying the potential deployment of advanced nuclear energy technologies that, while nascent, could be safer than conventional reactors.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We had previously announced our plans to build a pool of around 100 nuclear energy and safety experts.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We already now have over 40 such experts whose priority in the coming years is to work with our partners to assess the potential for deploying advanced nuclear energy technologies safely in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Taken together, the measures I have mentioned constitute a holistic set of decarbonisation efforts.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They maximise what is currently possible domestically, technologically and economically, while we work to advance the technologies and partnerships needed for the later phases of our decarbonisation journey.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The next question is how to help our businesses transition to this new economy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Ms Poh Li San, Mr Dennis Tan and Ms He Ting Ru asked about costs, opportunities and the circular economy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Ms He, in particular, talked about consumption-based emissions versus production-based emissions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I should explain that currently, the world operates on a production-based emissions system.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The entire United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) architecture is based around that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is the way that we count, officially, carbon emissions for each country.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And also, the methodologies for this are very well developed.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For consumption-based emissions, the methodologies are not standardised and they are not widely applied.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And in any case, they will not be directly applicable to our carbon account under the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But we are encouraging companies to start accounting for these things because, eventually, if carbon emission costs around the world rise, this will affect them also through their supply chain.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, they ought to know where their supply chain risks are.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are working with the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) and a consortium of partners to launch the Singapore Emission Factors Registry.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This helps businesses in Singapore track and report their carbon emissions more accurately by using a database of emissions factors developed based on Singapore's context.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Prior to this, most Singapore businesses had to rely on emission factors from international sources for emissions reporting, especially for Scope 3 emissions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But to remain competitive as an economy, we must take steps towards decoupling growth from emissions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That means, if we want to grow, we must decouple that from higher emissions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We must find a way of growing without the concomitant higher emissions that growth brings.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As we move towards a low-carbon future, businesses and economies that remain emissions intensive relative to their competitors will become less attractive.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, while there are costs in decarbonisation now, it is an investment in long-term survival and growth for our companies and also for Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are helping businesses decarbonise by supporting efforts to improve their energy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For instance, we have enhanced the Resource Efficiency Grant for manufacturing facilities and data centres, by lowering the minimum qualifying criteria to support more emissions reduction projects.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have also launched schemes to support businesses in sustainability reporting.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In addition, we have been working closely with the private sector to develop sectoral roadmaps to decarbonise each sector, seize new opportunities and remain competitive in the low carbon transition.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For example, we launched the Singapore Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint last year and, more recently, announced the Marine and Offshore Industry Plan.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These will guide us as we work together with companies in our key sectors in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We also want to become an AI hub.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) will say more about how we plan to green our data centres to achieve both economic growth and decarbonisation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As the demand for low-carbon goods and services increases, we can benefit by moving quickly to capture new markets.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have traditional strengths in marine and offshore.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Most of that has been in the oil and gas industries.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And now, there is a huge new opportunity in offshore wind.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: With the support of Enterprise Singapore, Singapore companies in the oil and gas sector are already finding success in pivoting towards providing critical products and services across the offshore wind value chain.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It has now grown to become one of the largest offshore wind support vessel owners globally, supporting clients across Asia Pacific and Europe.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There will also be new opportunities in resource efficiency and circularity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For example, we are supporting research to explore the use of captured carbon dioxide to produce building materials.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The transition will not be straightforward and is likely to be messy and uneven.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The reality is that we, as a global community, will make progress but may not collectively meet the 1.5°C goal.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment will say more about adaptations to rising urban heat, disruptions to food supplies and other impacts, which will be needed too.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Chairman, over our 60 years of Independence, we have always placed emphasis on a clean and green environment even as we developed and grew.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: With climate change, this challenge has now taken on a global dimension.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We cannot be sure what other countries will or will not do.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But we will secure Singapore's future, by doing our part to reduce emissions, by partnering our households and businesses in this transition, by taking steps to protect us from the effects of climate change, so that Singapore remains a sustainable, liveable and thriving country for all our citizens, ready to grasp the new opportunities in a low-carbon world.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, let us all work together and travel this journey together.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Are there any clarifications for Senior Minister Teo?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I am not so sure whether these clarifications will be answered by the Senior Minister Teo, but I will leave him to explain.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Regarding the cut that I just delivered on the regulations for AI, I heard the Senior Minister Teo referring to MDDI.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Is MDDI going to reply to my cut on carbon emissions regulations for AI?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I also asked about the concern that I have after Terminal 5 opens, when our Changi Airport flights may increase quite considerably and which will lead to an increase in aviation emissions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Yes, the Senior Minister Teo mentioned about the 1% sustainable aviation fuels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: But of course, compared to some other places, for example, I believe, Heathrow, I think it is about 10%, if I am not wrong.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Actually, I am just wondering, is the Senior Minister going to address that question I have?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Essentially, it is how will our sustainable air hub blueprint be stepped up in the next few years to mitigate the likely increase in aviation emissions after Terminal 5 opens?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: My third clarification, where in my Budget debate speech, I sought the Government's update on the green transition or the transition of our petrochemicals industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Where do we stand now in our journey, especially in light of the sale of the Shell assets in Jurong Island and Tuas last year?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Related to this is actually about the manpower transition for our workers in the petrochemical industry, but I am not sure whether the Ministry of Manpower will be dealing with this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Yes, indeed, Minister Chee will take the Member's questions on Terminal 5 and sustainable aviation fuels in the COS.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And also, for AI, MDDI will take that up with the Member.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They are not all there today, but that is the trajectory on which we are moving.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, we are a serious player in the sustainable aviation fuels area, but we must also understand that the pace at which we proceed should be aligned with the pace which the global players proceed and which our regional partners or competitors proceed, and we should not be too out of line with what they do.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On manpower transition, I will also leave that to the Ministry of Trade and Industry when they deal with that particular industrial sector.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: First, I would like the Senior Minister to clarify about whether there are any further details about timeline, for when this will be up and running.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I know that it has been launched, but also the details of when we are going to onboard various industries.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Second, whether the Senior Minister can give a bit more details about which sectors will be prioritised for this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: For the EU carbon border adjustment mechanism that I highlighted earlier, they target carbon intensive sectors, such as electricity, steel, cement and so on.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: So, I am just wondering whether we have a similar approach.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Chairman, I do not have the details on the timelines.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Because if we do not, what will happen is, when our exports reach the borders of those countries which have a carbon border adjustment mechanism, they will get taxed there.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And so, this has also been the reason why some of our neighbours have recently introduced their own carbon taxes, in order to make sure that they conform.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Mr Chairman, I have a question for Senior Minister Teo.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The Senior Minister mentioned that the carbon tax is an important enabler to incentivise businesses to go green and we know that the carbon tax has been projected to reach between $50 to $80 per tonne of carbon dioxide in the next five years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: But five years is not a very long time for businesses to plan ahead.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, that is why we have that indication that we are going to increase and also the range to which we are likely to increase it too.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, I think that will give businesses an opportunity to make their own assessments within the range that we are able to forecast right now.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I hope that that is sufficient for the time being, because those are sort of further out.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But as we approach those times when we are going to increase the carbon taxes, we will give them adequate advance notice, as we have done in the past.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I believe that is all the clarifications for Senior Minister Teo.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Couples often cite concerns about managing their work and family commitments.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This points both to the need to provide more affordable access to caregiving resources, such as childcare and migrant domestic workers (MDWs), as well as equipping couples in dual income families to perform well at work to maximise livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In this respect, how can the Government do more to support working parents with their caregiving needs?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can I ask what is the latest TFR in 2024?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Did it increase with the effect of the Dragon year last year?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If TFR has improved in 2024 due to the Dragon year effect, besides having more hopes for more babies for Singapore, will the Government consider commissioning research psychologists and behavioral scientists to conduct a study with interviews of parents who have had Dragon year babies to better understand and distill what are the underlying root beliefs that lead to the unusually better TFR in most Dragon years, despite all other circumstances, for example, high cost of living, lack of time, work and life stress, remaining the same in such years?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can the Government use such studies to better design public messaging and conditions that will be more conducive for Singaporean couples to have more babies?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Singapore Government do a more thorough study on the factors contributing to Israel's stable TFR and consider what can be adapted for Singapore?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a lower value against the global average of about 58%.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A lower ratio indicates less financial stress on working people and greater political stability.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The total age dependency ratio that the World Bank uses is the ratio of young and elderly dependents who are generally economically inactive, compared to the number of people of working age.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Despite this good data from the World Bank, with an ageing population and declining TFR, there is still cause for concern.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Two, where can young Singaporeans, grassroots advisors like me, grassroots organisations and educational institutions interested to support marriage and parenthood find accurate, age-appropriate and contextual information about fertility health of both women and men to increase public awareness and education on this important health topic?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Did we have more births from the Year of the Dragon?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the updated data on the number and ratio of working citizens to those who are retired?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened that the Government is providing greater support for parents who desire more children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be incentives to encourage and support young couples to have more children earlier?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the Government doing to help and support singles who are interested in marriage to meet potential partners?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For children of single mothers, I urge the Government to admit them into the Baby Bonus scheme and update legislation for their inheritance rights to their mothers' assets.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, a Singaporean whose wife is a Permanent Resident (PR) and having their first pregnancy is having a very stressful time trying to get a Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP) for his mother-in-law for long enough to provide both emotional and physical care to his wife who is having health and pregnancy complications.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The soon-to-be mother is terrified, this being her first pregnancy and by a health situation that requires her to have a prolonged period of recovery postpartum and more intensive care of the baby post-birth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The couple worries about the well-being of both mother and child and financial inadequacy if they cannot find suitable childcare and the wife needs to quit her job.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: With later marriages and pregnancies increasing the risks of complications and the absence of family members around to care for them, parenthood can be daunting and scary.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has valid concerns about aged grandparents having extended stay in Singapore, as it adds on to the country's potential eldercare burdens and costs if they are not financially supported.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Contribution amounts can be tiered according to the elderly parent's age and health condition – those with no chronic illnesses contribute less, while those with chronic illnesses contribute more.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And put in place annual mandatory health checks for each extension of the visit pass.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This way, foreign grandparents can continue being in their grandchildren's lives and be motivated to keep healthy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Those who are financially able can also contribute to this ParentCare Fund themselves.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: When they do return to their home countries in their last years, they can withdraw this fund for their own care.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This will provide a pool of funds should healthcare costs need to be incurred during their stay here or add to their retirement fund if unutilised, and allow couples and children to benefit from the presence and support of grandparents for as long as their health allows them to contribute.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I urge the Government to study this and make a win-win solution possible for transnational families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As families juggle demanding work schedules and caregiving duties, more substantial support structures are essential to help them manage both effectively.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What additional measures is the Government considering to ease caregiving pressures for working parents, especially those with young children?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Are there plans to enhance childcare accessibility, parental leave policies or flexible work arrangements (FWAs) to support families better?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond workplace policies, how can we strengthen community-based support networks to assist working parents in areas, such as after-school care, parental coaching or peer support groups?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we continue to encourage parenthood while supporting career aspirations, how will the Government ensure that working parents have the resources and flexibility to balance family and work commitments?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Tripartite Guidelines on FWA Requests were a welcome step.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My other colleagues and I in this House have asked about childcare leave, especially for families with many children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Large Families Scheme is a step in recognising the increased financial burden on larger families.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can the Government do more to support working parents with their caregiving needs?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, Members have called for additional childcare leave for parents with more children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But I also note the Government's position that we have already made major moves like the Shared Parental Leave recently, so we should give employers and businesses time to adjust to these moves first.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I myself have constituents who are employers and also constituents who are employees covering for colleagues on parental leave.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, it does take a whole village to support Singaporeans to start and raise families and I understand the need to strike a careful balance with any move.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, I wish to make a push today for just a bit more childcare leave and with a slightly different consideration.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because these eight days of annual closures are actually wonderful opportunities for young parents to use the time to bond with their young children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, for couples with more than one child in preschool, it is likely that all the young children will be attending the same preschool, with the same annual closure dates.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, it becomes all the more valuable for both parents to be able to align their childcare leave with the closure dates and allow the whole family to come and spend time together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, we should push for FWAs as the dominant solution to support parents with more children.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, you can take your six cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Josephine Teo shared in her reply that, "He spoke from the heart and won us with not just the strengths of his arguments but also the intensity of his conviction."

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Hany Soh, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will the Government further increase awareness of this risk and support Singaporeans in this area?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fertility Support SG, a non-profit self-help group, has shared with the People's Action Party (PAP) Women's Wing Policy Group, some best practices globally.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Japan, the government provides counselling and support services for all couples facing infertility, including emotional support and guidance on treatment options.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Australia has a national infertility support organisation that provides information, resources and peer support to couples and individuals.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Its various states have also integrated both public and private sector initiatives to support fertility treatments, often including financial subsidies as well as robust counselling services.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Certain states in the US, including New York, have mandated insurance companies to cover infertility treatments.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is the situation that my Woodgrove resident, Tina, is in.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Her medical fertility team has advised her to continue with her treatment even after the existing subsidies have been fully utilised as each cycle actually brings them closer to finding the optimal combination of medication and timing for successful conception.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Couples considering or expecting their first child would invariably feel overwhelmed or anticipate getting lost along their parenthood journey.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can the Government better support these parents and aspiring parents in their prenatal and parenthood journey?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I repeat my request for the Government to introduce, amongst other support schemes, a "Mommy's Milestone Booklet" to keep track and support an expectant mother's holistic well-being.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In our continuing drive towards being a smart and smarter nation, this booklet could also be issued in electronic format, comprising a side guide that updates parents about new developments in the parenthood journey, including getting value-for-money deals from parenthood-friendly businesses and perhaps even include a live chat function with human expertise or AI support where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I look forward to the Government's response, please.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, raising a large family is rewarding but challenging.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a father of five, I understand the sacrifices parents make.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is why I advocate a whole-of-society approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They need affordable housing and childcare, FWAs and strong community networks to share caregiving.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Parents fear a third child might stretch resources, disadvantaging their other children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond policy, we must foster a culture that values large families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Small efforts like family-friendly parking, restaurant accommodations and mentorship programmes signal support.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Investing in big families means investing in Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us build a society where families of all sizes thrive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a thoughtful initiative shaped by feedback from parents who emphasised the need for practicality, usefulness and aesthetic appeal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As the Minister highlighted, parents do not want just beautiful but impractical items.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They want something they could use and treasure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the deeper barriers – housing costs, childcare affordability, work-life balance – that prevent young families from growing?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, can we have more clarity on the gift's nature?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us ensure that this initiative is part of a broader effort to make raising a family in Singapore truly sustainable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This year, we celebrate 60 years of nation-building.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have come a long way as a people and a nation, and, together, we have built a Singapore that we can be proud of.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Dragon year effect has been diminishing over the years, reflecting the generational shifts in attitudes and priorities among young couples.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the updated ratio of working adults to retirees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A decade ago, there were six residents aged 20 to 64 years old supporting every elderly person aged 65 years and over.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A low fertility rate and an ageing population have significant implications on our economy and society.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As our local workforce growth slows, it will be increasingly challenging to sustain economic growth and maintain a dynamic economy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There will be fewer young people to support a growing elderly population.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Addressing our low TFR remains a national priority.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling suggested working with academics and studying other countries' practices to tackle low fertility.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are doing so and also regularly engage Singaporeans to develop policies that fit our local context.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As shared during the Motion on families earlier this month, we have a comprehensive suite of measures to support Singaporeans in their marriage and parenthood journey – from housing, healthcare, preschool and education to financial and work-life support.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have made significant enhancements in recent years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In 2023, we enhanced the Baby Bonus Cash Gift and contributions to the Child Development Account (CDA).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have reviewed and will be expanding the uses of CDA to better support parents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) will share more at their COS.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In 2024, we launched the Tripartite Guidelines on FWA Requests.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The enhanced Government-Paid Paternity Leave and new Shared Parental Leave announced by the Prime Minister last year will start from 1 April this year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This month, in Budget 2025, the Prime Minister announced the new Large Families Scheme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But for these policies to work, we need mindsets and culture to shift in tandem.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This requires support from everyone across society, as highlighted by Ms Ng Ling Ling.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Employers, supervisors and coworkers can all contribute to fostering a family-friendly workplace culture.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will foster the parent-child bond and it is good for the child's development, too.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We know it is not easy for employers to manage when their employees are away for an extended period.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is why it is so important for employees and employers to build mutual trust and play their part in making the leave provisions work for both parties.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Employees should discuss their leave plans and covering arrangements with their supervisors and coworkers as early as possible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the same time, managers and coworkers ought to be supportive and facilitative so parents feel reassured about taking time away from work.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Mr Louis Ng highlighted, fathers should be encouraged to fully utilise their paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One key step we have taken is to introduce employment protection for fathers on paternity leave from April this year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will study utilisation patterns and see how to better support fathers who encounter challenges in using their leave.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Various Members asked for further support for working parents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Suggestions include providing more leave for parents of preschoolers, those with pre-term and multiple births, larger families, as well as those seeking fertility treatment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At present, each working parent with a youngest child aged below seven years old has six days of paid childcare leave a year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This means a working couple would have a total of 12 days to tap on – more than the number of preschool closure days that Mr Xie Yao Quan mentioned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have also doubled Unpaid Infant Care Leave since 2024, where each working parent will have 12 days per parent per year, in the child's first two years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These parental leave provisions are provided on top of the parents' annual leave provisions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to review our parental leave provisions in consultation with parents and tripartite partners.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While we understand the desire for more childcare leave, any further leave enhancement has to be carefully considered and must strike a balance between the needs of different caregivers and the operational impact on employers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: More broadly, however, we do need employers to embrace more family-friendly workplace practices.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For instance, FWAs are an important form of support for parents with young children and other workers with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When implemented well, FWAs enable employees to balance their responsibilities both at work and at home.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With the implementation of the Tripartite Guidelines on FWA Requests from December last year, I hope that more employers will embrace FWAs as part of their core HR strategy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Employers are also encouraged to go beyond the legislated leave provisions to position themselves as employers of choice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, more than 4,000 employers have adopted the Tripartite Standard on Unpaid Leave for Unexpected Care Needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested incentivising businesses, to ensure their employees take parental leave.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In reality, new workplace norms are emerging and the younger generation of workers value greater work-life balance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If employers want to continue to attract and retain talent in their companies, their workplace practices will have to evolve.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, Adecco Group APAC Pte Ltd has an employee who will be eligible for the new Shared Parental Leave.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They plan to hire temporary and contract staff as covering manpower so that the employee can take her parental leave with peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When the employee returns to work, Adecco will also make available suitable FWAs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will allow the employee to balance her work and family commitments while still ensuring the company's work gets done.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng can rest assured that we will continue to work with employers to foster more family-friendly workplaces and encourage those who can, to go beyond what is mandated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The wider community can also play a part in supporting working parents, as Dr Wan Rizal highlighted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our Marriage and Parenthood Surveys show over a third of married couples aspire to have three or more children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, fewer married couples are having more than two children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some worry about having less time for each child.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Others may be daunted by the prospect of higher expenses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, parents receive more under the Baby Bonus Scheme and Parenthood Tax Rebate for each subsequent child they have.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But we want to give greater assurance to couples who wish to have larger families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Large Families Scheme will provide more financial support for large families for a start.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The LifeSG credits will provide sustained support for large families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Parents can use these credits to buy groceries at major supermarkets, or to top up the family's SimplyGo cards for public transport.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They can also be used to pay for rides from transport operators that accept NETS QR payment, like TADA and ComfortDelGro taxis.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will provide more information on how to access and use the credits later this year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We recognise large families also face other challenges, as highlighted by various Members during the Budget debate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, they may require larger housing, face difficulties getting around as a family, or worry about the costs of higher education that increase with more children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will study Members' suggestions on how to further support large families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng highlighted the need for whole-of-society support to shift norms and encourage larger families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We hope the Large Families Scheme will kickstart a societal movement to celebrate and support these families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have been engaging corporates to support the Large Families Scheme by offering privileges and deals for families with three or more children.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, to help larger families travel around more easily, private-hire services like Grab and Gojek will be offering discounts on bookings with their larger vehicles.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Car-sharing services like Tribecar and GetGo will be offering discounts on car rentals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: HomeTeamNS will be offering bundle promotions for tickets to their clubhouse family events, adventure and children's facilities, as well as discounted membership fees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: FairPrice Group will also be offering value bundles for large families to provide savings on essential groceries.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We encourage more corporates to join us in this movement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Together, let us make Singapore a conducive place for large families to thrive.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Hany Soh and Ms Ng Ling Ling highlighted the importance of raising awareness on fertility health issues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Fertility health can be a difficult topic to broach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We need to change mindsets and normalise conversations about fertility health and support couples who have fertility health concerns to seek help without fear of stigma.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The wider community can play an important role in this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ground-up efforts by groups like Fertility Support SG provide a safe space for couples facing infertility to share their experiences.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It also recently organised a fertility fair to raise awareness of the fertility health resources and support available.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To address the myths and misconceptions about fertility health, we collaborated with the Obstetrics and Gynaecology Society of Singapore to publish an article titled "Debunking 5 Myths of Fertility Health" on Health Hub.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It contains information on commonly faced fertility issues and provides useful resources for couples seeking help.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They can also tap on their MediSave for the treatment costs, up to a lifetime withdrawal limit of $15,000 per patient.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have made some progress in supporting fertility issues in Singapore, but more can be done.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With more Singaporeans marrying and having children later, as Ms Hany Soh and Mr Louis Ng pointed out, we may need to relook our support on this front.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Hany Soh spoke about providing more support for those who are expecting.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The antenatal journey can be daunting, especially for first-time parents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I have taken note of Ms Hany Soh's suggestions and we will look into them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We welcome further suggestions on how we can make the antenatal journey more positive for expecting couples.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This year, we celebrate our 60th year of Independence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng will be happy to hear that the gift represents our commitment towards building a Singapore Made for Families.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is also a symbol of our hopes and aspirations for our future generations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Many people have been asking about the SG60 Baby Gift.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I think it will address some of the curiosity that everyone is having.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The gift comes with a specially designed trolley bag which can double up as a travel case for the baby and contains a specially curated set of 10 commemorative and useful items, sourced from local brands and companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They include practical items like the straw cup set from local brand, Hegen, which comes with their patented adaptor cap to meet the babies' needs as they gain more independence feeding themselves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are educational items like storybooks by local authors featuring Becky Bunny, our mascot for the Families for Life movement, as well as a plushie of Becky Bunny.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We encourage parents to bond with their babies over these books and inspire a love for reading through them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Other items include play items that will help their babies in their growth and development, as well as items for parents to mark their precious moments with their little ones.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Students from LASALLE College of the Arts designed the artwork that you can see on the SG60 Baby Gift items.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Each gift set comes with a congratulatory letter from Prime Minister Wong.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We hope parents will find the gift meaningful and useful – to inspire their child in discovering the world around them, and to support parents in nurturing and caring for their child.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We hope that families will be able to join the event in their neighbourhood and get to know other young parents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As we celebrate SG60, allow me to highlight two values which have served us well over the last 60 years: openness and multiculturalism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These are fundamental aspects of who we are and key strengths that help us to make our way in the world.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Immigrants help to moderate the impact of low birth rates and ageing on the size and age profile of the citizen population.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to carefully manage the pace of immigration, taking into account factors, such as the falling TFR.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also granted around 35,000 new Permanent Residents, or PRs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The average number of new citizenships and new PRs granted annually over the past five years is slightly higher than that over the preceding period.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We remain committed to ensuring that our new citizens and PRs are well-integrated into our communities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We can all play our part to embrace the newcomers in our midst and help them to better understand our local norms and culture.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Over time, many of them become not just friends but also family.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Over the last decade, more than one-third of citizen marriages every year were transnational, meaning marriages involving a Singaporean and a foreigner.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One such transnational family is Kiren T and Angela Bueno's family.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Kiren, a Singaporean Indian, and Angela, a PR originally from the Philippines, met while working in the same children's ward in the National University Hospital.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They fell in love working and doing their in-house advanced diploma together and got married in 2016.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, they have two children, a boy and girl, aged nine and seven.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Many transnational couples make Singapore their home and over time, these foreign spouses become one of us.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Carrie Tan asked whether the Government could facilitate long-term visit passes, or LTVPs, for foreign parents of transnational couples, to help with the couple's parenting journey.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, Singapore Citizens and PRs can apply to sponsor their own foreign parents for an LTVP, subject to the prevailing criteria.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These LTVPs come with a validity of up to five years and can be renewed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This relatively long period provides some certainty to help transnational couples in planning their caregiving arrangements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to review our population strategies to ensure that they remain relevant in meeting our needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As we look to the next 60 years and beyond, let us work together to build stronger families, a more united society and a brighter future for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I have pushed the issue of childcare leave for a number of years now, but can I just have two requests for the Minister?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: One, can the Government do a public consultation to see how much support there is for the increase in childcare leave and how much is needed by families with children?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Two, whether we can do a consultation with businesses to understand again what concerns they have with regard to increasing childcare leave and what kind of support they hope from the Government when it comes again to increasing childcare leave?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think there is no doubt that if you ask parents, they would definitely like to have more childcare leave.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is when you speak to the employers that they have some concerns, not because they do not want to give childcare leave, but they are also grappling with the Tripartite Guidelines on FWA Requests, as well as the new Shared Parental Leave that we have also asked them to accommodate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I think, let them have some time to work through the Shared Parental Leave and the FWAs and it is not that additional childcare leave is a never, but it is really more a question of letting the employers and the businesses adjust and arrive at some equilibrium, before we start adding on to the things that they need to do.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling: Mdm Chairman, I thank the Minister for the very comprehensive updates.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I remember during the debate of the Motion for support of marriage and parenthood, the Minister explained the rationale of why the Government is reluctant to set a TFR target.
Ms Indranee Rajah: Mdm Chairperson, I appreciate the sentiment and I genuinely wish that it was so easy.
I could go and tell every newly-married woman, "I expect one child from you" or "Give me another child".
Or if you work it out, it will end up like 2.5 children or something like that.
But they also have their concerns and they have their needs, they have their worries and they have aspirations.

So, what we have tried to do is to approach it from the viewpoint of, "What are your concerns?" Your concerns are cost, your concerns are time, your concerns are housing, your concerns are work-life balance.
And then asking everybody to come on board – corporates, employers – to make Singapore more conducive.
Then, I think, if we send out a general call and we say, "Please have more children", then at least they feel a lot more assured in having children rather than just assigning them.
