speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, as late as May 2024, I asked the Prime Minister about the Government's assessment of the adequacy and effectiveness of existing measures to increase the attractiveness of the Singapore equities market, and whether the Government will take the lead in promoting our equities market by encouraging the privately-owned companies in which it holds equity through its investment vehicles to list in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Back then, Prime Minister Wong responded that notwithstanding the Government's efforts, the conditions remain challenging for the Singapore equities market, as they are for stock exchanges in many other countries, and that we have to be realistic about what we can do to change them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It was a disappointing response, but I was comforted to hear in August 2024 that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has set up a Review Group to recommend measures to strengthen equities market development in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, capital flow is more mobile and global than ever, seeking the best return wherever it may find.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our measures must be bold enough to bring our equity markets into the future, in order to give us the best chance of success.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I welcome the measures announced thus far but have some clarifications for the latest measures announced in February 2025.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As we all know, the Government has long held that directing GIC to invest in locally-listed firms is "not the solution" to improve the attractiveness of the local equity market and its mandate specifically excludes the Singapore market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is unlike Malaysia's Employees' Provident Fund (EPF), which is the largest investor in its domestic market, supporting Malaysian companies' capital needs and the economy as a whole.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How does MAS intend to use this seed funding to draw in investments from other investors?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the number of Singapore-focused equity funds have dwindled over the years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore represents just a small percentage of the Asia ex Japan and World indices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How does MAS intend to evaluate and allocate the funds to the fund managers, and how will these funds be disbursed?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Will there be sustained funding and cash injections for continued support of the equities market over the medium to long term?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I also wish to propose two key reforms to ensure long-term sustainability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This has been done before, through the listing of various Government-linked companies in the early years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even the Singtel Special Discounted Shares Scheme in 1993, aimed at making Singapore a share-owning society by giving Singaporean CPF members the opportunity to buy discounted Singtel shares.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Top of mind is PSA International, which pulled the plug on its IPO in 2002 after years of preparation and this plan was never revived.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Recently, Saudi Global Ports, in which PSA co-owns, is said to be aiming for an IPO worth up to US$1 billion in Riyadh too.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many families are excited to visit the new Mandai boardwalk and the upcoming Rainforest Wild Park.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure many will be excited to own a part of Mandai Wildlife Group.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Especially when we are looking at the long-term expansion of Changi Airport and Terminal 5, tapping the global capital markets is a key avenue in which we can fund Changi Airport Group in an efficient and sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, as MAS moves to move towards a more disclosure-based regime and a supposed pro-enterprise regulatory stance, it is imperative that we strengthen corporate governance standards and double down on investor education.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In 2023, Japan introduced what The Financial Times called a radical "name and shame" regime to drive better corporate governance and stock market valuations, particularly at listed companies with a price-to-book ratio of less than one.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Corporate reform since March 2023 following Tokyo Stock Exchange's directive for all companies to take "Action to Implement Management that is Conscious of Cost of Capital and Stock Price" has led to almost 90% of companies taking some kind of action by end-2024.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, since 2024, South Korea has also started to tackle the "Korea discount".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore can certainly take a leaf or two from them, by focusing on broad-based corporate governance reforms and implementing our own "value up" programme.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This will go hand in hand with a disclosure-based regime and address longstanding concerns on corporate governance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, Singapore investors, especially retail investors, need to be better equipped to make sound investment decisions and to question the board and management teams of the companies they have invested in.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This can only happen with a purposeful effort to strengthen investor education and empower retail investors to make informed investment decisions in a "buyer beware" regulatory regime.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, we need to do all we can if we want to revive our equity markets and this is our best chance, maybe our only chance.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I urge MAS to work with the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Singapore Prison Service in ensuring ex-offenders can open bank accounts.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A key challenge which many exchanges face is that global capital is heavily concentrated in the US and US-listed stocks currently account for around two-thirds of global stock market capitalisation.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Review Group is clear about our objectives and realistic about our goals.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Based on industry consultations, there are companies with a strong presence in Singapore and the region that might not be large enough to sustain investor interest post-listing if they were to list in the US.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These companies represent one key segment we could attract.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Review Group focused on strengthening the elements of our ecosystem to enhance its competitiveness and provide a well-functioning market for companies, including technology startups, to raise capital for their expansion.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The first set of measures span three mutually reinforcing pillars covering demand, supply and regulations.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On the EQDP implementation, MAS will start evaluating eligible fund managers and strategies in the next few months.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The EQDP will invest in a range of funds with a focus on Singapore stocks, including non-index component stocks.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These funds will be managed by fund managers with strong investment track record and capabilities in Singapore.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The fund strategies should be actively managed and commercially viable to attract capital from other investors.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MAS has experience in running programmes with both investment and market development objectives, and this is an extension of our approach in developing fund management capabilities in Singapore.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The feedback from the industry, so far, has been more encouraging than how Mr Chua has described it.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think other industry participants and stakeholders have given more positive comments about this move.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But whether it works or not, let us see.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will do our best and see whether this will help to grow the local fund management industry and also attract more investor liquidity.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, listing decisions will be made by the companies based on their commercial objectives.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We should allow this and not impose requirements for the companies to list on SGX, as it is more important for our overall economic competitiveness to preserve Singapore's attractiveness to the founders of these companies and the global investors who invest in them.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On the regulatory front, Mr Louis Chua's description of the Review Group's approach does not represent the full picture.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I hope this is not deliberate as it would otherwise be rather unfair to the Review Group and our workstream members, who include eminent industry leaders, such as Mr Neil Parekh.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: While regulation will be more focused and facilitative of listings, we will continue to uphold high corporate governance standards.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We stressed this a couple of times during our media conference and also in our reports.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Review Group also said that in the next phase of our review, we will look at initiatives to uplift companies' capabilities in shareholder engagement and sharpen their focus on shareholder value.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will enhance avenues for investor recourse and will take robust enforcement action against market misconduct.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, research coverage will be enhanced, to support investors to make better informed investment decisions.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As we embark on the next phase, the Review Group will continue to seek feedback and work closely with industry partners to co-create solutions and strengthen our foundations to give Singapore the best chance to attract listings and grow investor interest.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To promote financial inclusion, MAS has worked with major retail banks to offer Limited Purpose Bank Accounts (LPBAs).

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These address the basic banking needs of most ex-offenders and other persons whom banks have assessed to pose higher financial crime risks.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With LPBAs, individuals can receive salaries and government payouts, and make payments.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Banks monitor LPBA use more closely to ensure only funds from agreed sources are received and to detect suspicious transactions.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Banks will assess each case individually to decide whether to offer LPBAs and they have offered LPBAs to ex-offenders of serious financial crimes where the risks are manageable.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Banks may also decline to open an account for individuals who are assessed to pose unacceptable risks that cannot be mitigated by the LPBA's safeguards, such as those who repeatedly allow bank accounts to be misused, have violated financial sanctions or are unwilling to cooperate with the bank's due diligence.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We encourage individuals to provide the necessary information to banks to allow proper due diligence to be carried out.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This balances financial inclusion against the risk of our financial system being abused, which would then be to the public's detriment.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: She had continued to use her bank accounts to receive funds from people she did not know, despite repeated warnings from the Commercial Affairs Department not to do so.

speaker: ﻿The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat

text: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member): As bank accounts have now more or less become a necessity, is there any recourse for any individual or even business if they are unsuccessful in their application for bank accounts with all the banks?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms He Ting Ru: Madam, Singapore's research and development (R&D) landscape has a reputation for efficiency and the announcements in this year's Budget undoubtedly add to our strengths in physical infrastructure.

speaker: The Chairman
text: However, there is room to nurture truly visionary scientific research backed by the idea that detours and exploratory science can yield the most disruptive impact with a longer horizon.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Some might ask, why invest in exploratory research given our resource restraints?

speaker: The Chairman
text: The goal is not to supplant applied research but to increase our offerings to create a fertile ground to encourage potential breakthroughs that may only emerge years after.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In this vein, Switzerland's Spark scheme offers lessons.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The scheme explicitly minimises bureaucracy and encourages high-risk, unconventional ideas comprising four main points.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It welcomes proposals that challenge existing norms or lacks extensive data and expressly accepts projects that traditional schemes may deem too speculative.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Third, double-blind proposal evaluation where applicants and evaluators remain anonymous, guarding against bias that may result from individual or institutional prestige overshadowing each proposal's intrinsic merits.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In Spark's eyes, even projects that fail can may mined for valuable insights, noting the explorations are essential even when outcomes are unclear.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In Singapore's context, adopting a Spark-like model means carving out a dedicated stream for high-risk, early-stage exploration where high-risk research is explicitly insulated from more traditional performance measures.

speaker: The Chairman
text: A possible pilot would be to create open problem platforms with prizes, like global cryptography or single-cell biology competitions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: After all, the essence of science is uncertainty and real breakthroughs rarely proceed linearly.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Our system has to accommodate exploration and dead ends and to allow impossible experiments.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I also hope that we could consider two further measures in Singapore: allowing principal investigators (PI) to use PhD students for high-risk projects and permitting PIs to use a proportion of grant funds towards exploratory work.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The aim here would be to stimulate original ideas rather than confining researchers to incremental pursuits.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Meanwhile, the 2024 Frontier Competitive Research Programme grant call announced in May 2024 focuses on use-inspired basic research.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Could the Minister clarify how substantial the commitment is, which projects have secured support and how is this publicised to all scientists?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Is this a sustained initiative or a one-off call?

speaker: The Chairman
text: To be a truly world-leading R&D research hub, Singapore has to invest in exploration that may time to bear fruit or even fail.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I hope that the ideas above will contribute to policies that reflect the thinking necessary for Singapore to sustain our competitive edge in an uncertain global innovation race.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Quantum computing promises exponential improvements in simulating physical systems and solving complex problems faster than classical computers.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I seek greater clarity on our quantum roadmap.

speaker: The Chairman
text: First, Singapore is currently focused on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) machines, which rely on many short, error-prone runs and statistical processing of noisy outputs.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Are there plans to pivot or also pursue FTQC?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Second, under the photonics and control electronics vertical of the National Quantum Processor Initiative (NQPI), how does the National Quantum Office plan to develop auxiliary industries, namely controls, readout and hardware-based error correction, to support next-generation quantum processors?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Third, NQPI's science verticals focus on trapped ions and neutral atom arrays.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Could the Minister clarify why superconducting qubits promising synergies with our semiconductor industry's cleanroom fabrication processes were excluded?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Fourth, QKD has been strongly promoted by the Government and Temasek.

speaker: The Chairman
text: However, QKD requires specialised, expensive hardware, whereas post-quantum cryptography (PQC) needs only software updates.

speaker: The Chairman
text: In this light, what is the view over our continued significant investments in QKD?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Does the Government foresee regional QKD networks, possibly via low Earth orbit satellites and how would such efforts compare against simpler, cheaper PQC solutions?

speaker: The Chairman
text: I can see you are very eager to move your cut.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In my Budget debate speech, I touched on how Singapore is operating in an increasingly challenging geopolitical environment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I have regularly highlighted, in this House, that it is important for Singapore to ensure that our Public Service officers have broad perspectives so that they are equipped to take on not only today's challenges but challenges of the future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is even more crucial now, with rising tensions between big global powers and the threat of impending trade wars.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What critical cross-cutting and diverse capabilities should the Public Service prioritise in developing its officers to ensure that they are future-ready?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How is the Public Service enhancing its officers' international exposure, competencies and understanding of global trends?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What opportunities exist for officers to gain international experience through overseas postings or exchanges?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, what are the Public Service's strategies to foster engagements and build relationships with international partners?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What opportunities are there for regular dialogue and collaboration with foreign public service counterparts, to anticipate global shifts?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Chairman, our citizens' needs are becoming more complex and interconnected, crossing traditional Government boundaries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: While we have developed new services, the main challenge is integrating them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: We must ensure help is accessible without obstacles and bureaucracy, providing solutions and support instead.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: In previous debates, I spoke about the sheer number of Government apps and systems, about how, for too many Singaporeans, finding the right service feels like navigating a maze.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: I emphasised the necessity of transitioning from an agency-centric approach to a citizen-centric model, because no one should have to struggle through Government silos just to get the help they need.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: No one should be left wondering where to turn when services should already be meeting them where they are.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: How do we move from complexity to clarity?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: It must understand that our citizens' needs do not exist in isolation and neither should the solutions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: This means bundling services across multiple agencies, proactively connecting the dots at every stage of life and it means more than just adopting new technology.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: It means adopting a new way of thinking, a mindset shift, a commitment to breaking down silos so that no Singaporean is left behind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: That is how we build a Government that is not just effective, but responsive; not just efficient, but compassionate; a Government that does not just serve the people, but truly empowers them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Singapore faces significant demographic changes in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our workforce is rapidly ageing, alongside rapid economic and technological changes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is in recognition that with higher life expectancy, many older officers may wish to stay active, including being meaningfully engaged at work for longer, though in different ways.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While policy changes are being enacted to enable officers to continue working for longer, how can the Public Service ensure that individual officers on the ground feel confident, well-equipped and adequately prepared for their extended careers as job demands will change in the future?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: What specific programmes and resources are being put in place to empower public officers as they navigate longer working lives?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: How can we help officers build good transition skills and strike a balance between leveraging their wealth of experience while remaining able, agile and adaptable in a rapidly-evolving work landscape?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chair, we thank Members for their various questions and suggestions on how our Public Service can do better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: She asked how we support exploratory scientific research and about our approach to quantum research.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In any research, particularly initial research, there will be many competing ideas.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For instance, the mRNA vaccines that were crucial to fighting COVID-19 are a good example.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The vaccines were enabled by decades of work in mRNA therapeutics, which many initially regarded as unpromising.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: No one knew then the role it would eventually play in a global pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In R&D, success requires carefully balancing continuity in commitment and investment, with the ability to pivot decisively when the need arises.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There is no one method in managing the complexity of different fields of research, different levels of research, different maturities or readiness-to-market levels of research.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, it is not a one method or a one-size-fits all.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Different research areas with different time horizons, different challenges, require different management methods.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We review our programmes regularly, pivot them when necessary, or double down on efforts that show strong promise when circumstances evolve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We can only have such optionalities if we have built up our capabilities and talent intentionally.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I must also explain that in making such decisions, we do not just rely on our own expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Because in many of these emerging fields, we may not have all the expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And this is the reason why the National Research Foundation and our research institutes make sure that they have extensive global networks with different panels of advisors that can give us their different perspectives for us to make a considered decision.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And we have different councils, comprising both local and foreign experts in different fields to give us those advice that we need.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ms He asked about the possible technical approaches, including our current areas of focus as well as industry development efforts to build our quantum capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to adjust when needed and make judgements, taking into account the evolving landscape, our capabilities, what we have achieved and what others have achieved.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Also, we keep a keen eye on where others are investing in, so that we can focus on the areas that we will have a competitive advantage.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I would also like to assure Members that the key Government agencies and research offices are keeping a close watch on all of these, internal and external developments, in consultation with both our local and international scientific panels, and we are not wedded to any particular focal area or approaches.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But what we must do, carefully, is to build up the capabilities to allow us to have the suite of optionalities to pivot or double down as the circumstances evolve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And for Ms He's suggestions, we will be happy to take into account her suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If she has scientific papers that she feels will benefit our considerations, we welcome her to let us know and we will convey this to the National Research Foundation and our panel of scientific advisors to take a look at this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: More important than just building own talent pool and expertise, we must also grow our ecosystem of research institutes, industries and workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And when we say this, I do not just mean growing the capabilities in-house or only in this country.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Very often, in today's R&D environment, we will need to leverage on the networks that we are able to access in the global environment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: No one country, not even the biggest countries of India, China or US, will work alone necessarily in many of these cutting-edge areas and that is what we are committed to do.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And in a more fragmented world, we must also ride on the opportunity for us to play the role to bring people from different backgrounds together and that is one area of our competitive advantage.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This will then position Singapore strategically to contribute where we can and take advantage of the opportunities, be it in quantum technologies or other areas.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Now, let me address Ms Hazel Poa's cut, on behalf of the Prime Minister, on EBRC.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The current terms of reference provide some stability in our electoral landscape by having a balance in the proportion of GRCs and SMCs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Having Members of Parliament serving a broadly similar number of electors on average as the last election will enable Members in the coming Parliament to continue to serve and represent their residents effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As for greater transparency for its recommendations, we discussed this extensively during the debate on the Motion that Ms Poa and Mr Leong Mun Wai tabled in Parliament last August.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We do not intend to repeat the debate today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Suffice to say that we should avoid imposing requirements or instructions on EBRC that are too prescriptive, but to give EBRC, which comprises senior civil servants with the relevant professional knowledge and expertise, the space to do their work independently and objectively, without fear or favour.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next, Mr Melvin Yong asked how we would prepare the Public Service workforce to tackle the multifaceted challenges of the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our Public Service has achieved much for Singapore and Singaporeans since 1965.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Today, we are known for our efficiency, innovation and our ethos, from meritocracy to incorruptibility.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, Singapore has been ranked within the top five in the World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators on Government Effectiveness since 2014 and topped Oxford University's inaugural Blavatnik Index of Public Administration in 2024.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But having said that, we are not complacent and we must not be complacent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The once familiar rules-based international security and economic orders are fracturing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Achieving survival and success for Singapore and Singaporeans will require fresh approaches in the way we do things, not just internally but also how we connect with the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our people's aspirations, as Mr Yip Hon Weng says, have also changed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They have gone up, while our manpower resource base remains tight.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And we will constantly need to review the way we build our capabilities, execute and deliver.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, we must deepen our perspectives of the world and strengthen linkages with partners beyond our Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Public Service delivery does not happen in a vacuum, nor does it only depend on us looking inwards at our own issues.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat mentioned, for Singapore to remain successful, our Public Service must deeply appreciate the fast-evolving external context which we have to operate in.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must remain engaged with our international counterparts through active participation in international forums, exchange and training programmes, and we must keep in close touch with what is happening in many international agencies because the decisions that they make there can have significant impact on what we can or cannot do, even in our domestic context.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And this is where we will continue to send relevant officers to many of these international organisations for us to touch base with the latest thinking and build those networks that are necessary for our continued survival and success.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To this end, we aspire to send more officers beyond the Public Service and beyond Singapore, to understand and build those linkages to further the cause for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Just as an example, National Environment Agency officer, Khairunnisa Binte Yahya, has first-hand experience of this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: She was attached to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) as an Air Pollution Expert.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: She shares expertise and develops solutions for air pollution with UNDP partners, enhancing Singapore's global partnerships in environmental sustainability and climate resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Khairunnisa has gained insights into the UNDP's strategies which informs our efforts to improve Singapore's air quality.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: More importantly, she has built up a network, which she can call upon in time to come.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: A personal assistant at the Ministry of Social and Family Development, she pursued her passion for social work by obtaining a Singapore University of Social Sciences degree.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: After attending a CareerFitness workshop in 2023, she is now set for an attachment with Child Protection Services to apply her new skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To further reap the career longevity dividend, we will continue to tap on the Public Service Retirees Network, which provides job and volunteer opportunities, to harness their wealth of experiences and add resilience to our system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, our ServiceSG omni-channel strategy is not just about bringing different services together.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is about how we rewire our processes to deliver services more efficiently and yet, be more aligned with the way our people expect their service journey to be.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As we continue to streamline and digitise our services, we will certainly not leave those less digitally-savvy behind.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This requires a mindset shift from Ministry or agency-centricity, to a people-centricity and whole-of-Government perspective.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is a digital-first, but not a digital-only service that we are aiming for.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Third, we must strengthen team development for a more complex and challenging operating environment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And this is slightly different from how we have done things in the past.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In the Public Service, we have always focused on the development of the individual and this remains valid.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Going forward, we need to go beyond developing just the individual.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to strengthen the way we develop the teams and compose the team with diverse abilities, with people from diverse backgrounds and perspectives.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our ability to compose teams with diverse abilities to resolve and pre-empt problems is critical as challenges become more complex and interlinked.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: One, for our Public Service to maintain a sense of perspective, to not just be able to understand our own challenges deeply, but to have a view of how the world is evolving, because the rules are changing fast.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And unless we are plugged in, we might be overtaken or bypassed by other people making rules beyond our shores.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Build our teams with people with the courage and the know-how to pivot and change course when the need arises, to pre-empt problems.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, Chairman, we do not take for granted our strong track record and will naturally enable our success tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Indeed, we believe, as a Public Service, that we should be continuously vigilant to our fast-changing world order and domestic expectations, and constantly challenge ourselves to evolve faster.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is not just about solving today's problems better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is about anticipating tomorrow's challenges earlier to find those solutions before the problem arises.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is, perhaps, something that we have taken for granted.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In many countries, they, too, have people in their public service that have very strong convictions and good ideas on what they want to achieve, but they do not necessarily have the ability to do this and to do it well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And that is because they do not have the continuity in perspective, that allows them to think long term.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is something that we have, this is something that we cherish and this is a competitive advantage for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chair, I have shared how we will deepen our external linkages, deliver integrated services and strengthen our teams.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we do this well, if we do not become complacent, I am quite sure this will be a Public Service that we can all be proud of and this will be a Public Service that will partner us to SG100 and beyond.

speaker: The Chairman:
text: Ms Poh Li San, would you like to withdraw your cut?
